herbs.name: Ashwagandha
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda as a rasayana for general vitality and the wellbeing of the nervous system.

safetyFlags.note: NCCIH advises avoiding ashwagandha during pregnancy and not using it while breastfeeding.
Rare but sometimes severe liver injury (usually cholestatic, appearing within weeks to months) has been reported with ashwagandha supplements in several countries.
May raise thyroid hormone levels; cases of thyrotoxicosis and painless thyroiditis have been reported. NCCIH advises against use in people with thyroid disorders.
NCCIH advises against use in people with autoimmune conditions (immune-stimulating activity).
NCCIH advises against use by people about to have surgery (possible additive sedation with anaesthesia).
Short-term use (up to about 3 months) appears reasonably safe; long-term safety is not established.

interactions.effect: May raise thyroid hormone levels and add to the effect of levothyroxine, so thyroid levels may move out of range.
interactions.mechanism: Increases serum T3/T4 in a randomised trial; case reports of thyrotoxicosis.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, your doctor may want to re-check thyroid blood tests.

interactions.effect: May push thyroid hormone levels up and work against antithyroid medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Thyroid-stimulating effect (raised T3/T4 in trial; thyrotoxicosis case reports).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May work against medicines that dampen the immune system.
interactions.mechanism: Immune-stimulating activity; NCCIH lists immunosuppressants among possible interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May add to drowsiness from sleeping pills or sedatives.
interactions.mechanism: GABA-mimetic / sedative activity in preclinical studies; NCCIH lists sedatives among possible interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May change how well anti-seizure medicines work or add to drowsiness.
interactions.mechanism: NCCIH lists anticonvulsants among possible interactions; GABA-ergic activity shown in animals.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May lower blood sugar further when taken with diabetes medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Glucose-lowering effect seen in animal studies and small clinical studies; NCCIH lists diabetes medicines among possible interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often and know the signs of low blood sugar.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Side effects such as stomach upset, muscle pain or diarrhoea were reported when combined with some antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: Reported in a retrospective pharmacovigilance chart review (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine); mechanism unclear.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May add to sedation from anaesthesia.
interactions.mechanism: NCCIH advises against use before surgery; sedative activity.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon, anaesthetist and dentist that you take it. It is commonly advised to stop the herb about 2 weeks before planned surgery; ask your doctor.

herbs.name: Turmeric (incl. curcumin supplements)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda and Indian cooking for the general wellbeing of the skin, digestion and joints.
commonProducts: Bioavailable curcumin formulations (e.g. Meriva, BCM-95, Theracurmin)

safetyFlags.note: Liver injury (often hepatocellular, sometimes autoimmune-like) has been reported with turmeric/curcumin supplements, especially highly bioavailable or piperine-enhanced products; amounts used in food are not a concern.
Supplement doses may be unsafe in pregnancy; EMA does not recommend medicinal use in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
EMA advises against medicinal use with bile-duct obstruction, gallstones or liver disease (stimulates bile flow / gallbladder contraction).
Curcumin has antiplatelet and anticoagulant effects in laboratory studies.
Loose turmeric powder has been found adulterated with lead chromate in South Asia and linked to lead exposure, including in the US.
High-dose turmeric has been linked to iron-deficiency anaemia in a case report (curcumin binds iron).

interactions.effect: May increase the effect of warfarin-type blood thinners and raise the risk of bleeding (raised INR reported).
interactions.mechanism: Antiplatelet/anticoagulant activity of curcumin; a probable case of raised INR with a vitamin K antagonist (fluindione).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Watch for unusual bruising or bleeding. Tell your surgeon or dentist you take it; it is commonly advised to stop the herbal product about 2 weeks before planned surgery. Your INR may need to be checked more often.

interactions.effect: May add to the bleeding risk of newer blood thinners.
interactions.mechanism: Curcumin antiplatelet/anticoagulant activity in lab studies; additive effect is theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Watch for unusual bruising or bleeding. Tell your surgeon or dentist you take it; it is commonly advised to stop the herbal product about 2 weeks before planned surgery.

interactions.effect: May add to the effect of antiplatelet medicines and increase bleeding risk.
interactions.mechanism: Curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation in lab studies; in rats it changed clopidogrel levels without changing platelet effect.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Watch for unusual bruising or bleeding. Tell your surgeon or dentist you take it; it is commonly advised to stop the herbal product about 2 weeks before planned surgery.

interactions.effect: May add to bleeding risk, including stomach bleeding, with NSAID painkillers.
interactions.mechanism: Additive antiplatelet effect; theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise tacrolimus blood levels (kidney harm reported in one case), although another monitored patient showed no change.
interactions.mechanism: Probable CYP3A4/P-gp inhibition by curcumin; raised tacrolimus levels in rats and one case report; a second case found no effect at culinary doses.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you take tacrolimus or cyclosporine, levels may need extra monitoring.

interactions.effect: Curcumin lowered blood levels of tamoxifen and its active form endoxifen, which might reduce its effect.
interactions.mechanism: Clinical PK study in breast-cancer patients: endoxifen AUC fell 7.7% with curcumin and 12.4% with curcumin + piperine.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Tell your cancer team about any curcumin supplement.

interactions.effect: May add to the glucose-lowering effect of glibenclamide (glyburide).
interactions.mechanism: Small clinical study: curcumin altered glyburide levels and lowered glucose further (no hypoglycaemia observed).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often.

interactions.effect: Curcumin reduced absorption of the beta-blocker talinolol in volunteers, which could reduce its effect.
interactions.mechanism: Clinical PK study: talinolol AUC fell about one third after 6 days of curcumin (transporter-mediated).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May change blood levels of medicines that are moved by P-gp/BCRP transporters.
interactions.mechanism: Curcumin altered talinolol (P-gp) and sulfasalazine (BCRP) exposure in human studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May add to the risk of liver injury with other medicines that can affect the liver.
interactions.mechanism: Turmeric/curcumin is itself linked to rare liver injury; additive risk theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: High doses may reduce iron absorption.
interactions.mechanism: Curcumin is an iron chelator; iron-deficiency anaemia reported with high-dose turmeric.
interactions.advice: Ask your doctor or pharmacist; consider taking iron at a different time of day from turmeric supplements.

interactions.effect: May add to bleeding risk around surgery.
interactions.mechanism: Antiplatelet activity; theoretical.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon, anaesthetist and dentist that you take it. It is commonly advised to stop the herb about 2 weeks before planned surgery; ask your doctor.

herbs.name: Guggul
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, usually as purified resin in guggulu formulations, for the general wellbeing of joints and metabolism.

safetyFlags.note: Skin rash (hypersensitivity) was noticeably more common with guggulipid than placebo in a randomised trial.
Guggulsterone stimulated thyroid function in rats; relevance in people is uncertain.
Guggulsterone binds steroid hormone receptors (oestrogen, progesterone and others); use in pregnancy is not supported by safety data.
Acute liver failure has been reported with a multi-ingredient 'fat burner' that contained guggul (cause not attributable to guggul alone).

interactions.effect: May reduce absorption and effect of propranolol and diltiazem.
interactions.mechanism: Single 1 g dose of gugulipid significantly reduced Cmax and AUC of propranolol and diltiazem in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, have your blood pressure and heart rate checked.

interactions.effect: May reduce blood levels of diltiazem and beta-blockers used for heart rhythm.
interactions.mechanism: Reduced bioavailability of diltiazem and propranolol in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May lower blood levels of medicines broken down by CYP3A4, making them less effective.
interactions.mechanism: Guggulsterone activates the pregnane X receptor and induces CYP3A in lab studies; not confirmed in people.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May change thyroid function tests or levothyroxine needs.
interactions.mechanism: Thyroid-stimulating action of Z-guggulsterone in rats.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May work against antithyroid medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Thyroid-stimulating action of guggulsterone in rats; theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May interfere with hormone-based medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Guggulsterone binds oestrogen, progesterone and other steroid receptors in vitro; clinical relevance unknown.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Giloy / Heart-leaved moonseed
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda as a rasayana for general vitality and the wellbeing of the body's natural defences.

safetyFlags.note: Multicentre case series from India (especially during COVID-19 'immunity booster' use) linked giloy to liver injury, often autoimmune-like. The Ministry of Ayush disputes the link, citing possible plant misidentification.
May unmask or trigger autoimmune-like hepatitis; caution in people with autoimmune conditions.
Glucose-lowering activity in animal studies.

interactions.effect: May add to the risk of liver injury with medicines that can affect the liver.
interactions.mechanism: Giloy linked to autoimmune-like liver injury in case series; additive risk theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report tiredness, dark urine or yellow eyes promptly.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise glibenclamide levels and lower blood sugar further.
interactions.mechanism: In rats, 14-day giloy extract increased glibenclamide bioavailability and reduced clearance; CYP2C9 inhibition in vitro.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often.

interactions.effect: May lower blood sugar further with diabetes medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Hypoglycaemic activity of giloy alkaloids in animals.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often and know the signs of low blood sugar.

interactions.effect: May lower blood sugar further with diabetes medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Hypoglycaemic activity of giloy alkaloids in animals.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often and know the signs of low blood sugar.

interactions.effect: May slightly raise levels of medicines broken down by CYP3A4.
interactions.mechanism: Mild CYP3A4 inhibition by stem extract in vitro (stronger for its protoberberine alkaloid fraction); not shown in people.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May slightly raise levels of medicines broken down by CYP2C9.
interactions.mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition in human liver microsomes at high concentrations; not shown in people.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May slightly raise levels of medicines broken down by CYP2C19.
interactions.mechanism: CYP2C19 inhibited by giloy extract in rat and human liver microsomes (weaker than CYP2C9/CYP2D6); not shown in people.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Chebulic myrobalan
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the digestive system and as a rasayana (rejuvenative) herb.

interactions.effect: May add to the effect of other laxatives, causing loose stools or cramping.
interactions.mechanism: Additive laxative effect (Triphala/haritaki described as laxative at normal doses, purgative at high doses).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.mechanism: Triphala (containing haritaki) weakly inhibited CYP3A4 in vitro; in contrast, chebulinic acid induced several CYP enzymes in rats. Direction and clinical relevance unknown.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory alter levels of CYP2D6-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Triphala weakly inhibited CYP2D6 in vitro (high IC50 values); no human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory raise levels of omeprazole-type medicines.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Belleric myrobalan
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the respiratory and digestive systems, most often as one of the three fruits of Triphala.

safetyFlags.note: Mainly consumed within Triphala, which is laxative at normal doses; may cause loose stools.

interactions.effect: May add to the effect of other laxatives when taken as Triphala.
interactions.mechanism: Additive laxative effect of Triphala.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory alter levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Individual Triphala components, including T. bellirica, inhibited rat liver CYP activity in vitro; Triphala inhibited CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 weakly. No human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Kutki / Picrorhiza
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the liver and digestive system.

safetyFlags.note: Very bitter herb with limited human safety data; standardised extracts (picroliv) are biologically active on the immune system in animal studies.

interactions.effect: Could in theory work against immune-suppressing medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Picroliv (iridoid glycoside fraction) stimulated antibody and cell-mediated immune responses in mice; no human interaction data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Especially relevant after an organ transplant.

interactions.effect: Could in theory alter levels of CYP2C-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Picroside II (a kutki constituent) did not inhibit human liver microsomal CYPs in vitro, but repeated dosing inhibited CYP2C activity in rats.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory alter levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Low-dose picroside II increased CYP3A activity in rats; human relevance unknown.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Andrographis / Green chiretta
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the liver, digestion and seasonal immunity.

safetyFlags.note: Australia's regulator (TGA) has received hundreds of reports of hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis with Andrographis products, including a fatal case, and reactions occurred in people who had used it before without problems. In 2026 the TGA removed it from ingredients permitted in new listed medicines.
Not recommended in pregnancy: animal studies report anti-fertility and pregnancy-terminating effects; EMA HMPC could not establish a monograph because of insufficient data.
Acute kidney injury has been reported in China with intravenous andrographolide preparations (not oral herb); relevance to oral use is uncertain.
Common non-serious side effects in trials are gastrointestinal and skin reactions.

interactions.effect: May increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
interactions.mechanism: Andrographolide increased warfarin exposure in rats and Andrographis constituents inhibit platelet aggregation in vitro; a rat study with the Kan Jang combination found no significant warfarin effect, so data conflict.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Check INR more often if you start or stop the herbal product.

interactions.effect: May add to the blood-thinning effect of antiplatelet medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Andrographolide and 14-deoxy-11,12-didehydroandrographolide inhibit human platelet aggregation in vitro.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Possible added bleeding tendency around surgery.
interactions.mechanism: Theoretical, based on in vitro antiplatelet activity.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist about this herb; ask your doctor whether to pause the herbal product before planned surgery.

interactions.effect: May add to blood-pressure-lowering medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Hypotensive effect of extracts and diterpenoids in rats; no human interaction data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase glibenclamide (glyburide) levels and the risk of low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: Andrographolide increased glyburide bioavailability and hypoglycaemic effect in diabetic rats, attributed to CYP3A4 inhibition.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: May raise levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Extracts inhibit CYP3A4 in human liver microsomes and reduce CYP3A expression in human hepatocytes (summarised by EMA HMPC).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise levels of CYP2C9-metabolised medicines (e.g. warfarin, some sulfonylureas).
interactions.mechanism: Extracts inhibit CYP2C9 (tolbutamide hydroxylation) in human liver microsomes in vitro (summarised by EMA HMPC).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May change theophylline levels (direction unclear).
interactions.mechanism: In rats, andrographolide increased theophylline clearance, while whole extract slowed elimination at higher theophylline doses; andrographolide induces CYP1A in mouse hepatocytes.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory work against immune-suppressing medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Immunostimulant activity of andrographolide and extracts in experimental studies; no human interaction data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Moringa / Drumstick tree
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda and as a food for general nutritional wellbeing.

safetyFlags.note: Generally well tolerated and not linked to liver enzyme rises, but implicated in one case of acute anicteric hepatitis.
Used as a galactagogue; no serious short-term effects seen in nursing mothers or infants, but long-term infant data are lacking.
Leaf powder lowered blood glucose in small human studies.

interactions.effect: May add to glucose-lowering medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Glucose-lowering effects of leaf preparations in small human and animal studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: May add to glucose-lowering effect, with some risk of low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: Additive pharmacodynamic effect inferred from human glucose-lowering data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: May add to insulin's glucose-lowering effect.
interactions.mechanism: Additive pharmacodynamic effect inferred from human glucose-lowering data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: May add slightly to blood-pressure-lowering medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Moringa leaves lowered postprandial blood pressure in a small human study.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory alter thyroid hormone balance.
interactions.mechanism: Leaf extract lowered T3 and raised T4 in rats, suggesting reduced T4-to-T3 conversion; no human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Unlikely to change nevirapine levels at food-like doses.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory raise levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines at high extract doses.
interactions.mechanism: Leaf extracts and isolated constituents inhibit CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 in vitro; a human nevirapine study showed no meaningful effect.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory raise levels of CYP2D6-metabolised medicines at high extract doses.
interactions.mechanism: Leaf extracts inhibit CYP2D6 in vitro; no human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory reduce the effect of anticoagulants.

herbs.name: Black pepper (piperine)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda and cooking for general wellbeing of digestion, and as an ingredient that enhances the uptake of other herbs.

safetyFlags.note: Piperine is a 'bioavailability enhancer': it can raise blood levels of many medicines and of other supplements (for example, curcumin levels rose about 20-fold with 20 mg piperine).
Dietary pepper is compatible with breastfeeding; no studies of piperine supplements in nursing mothers.

interactions.effect: May raise blood levels of phenytoin and carbamazepine, increasing the risk of side effects such as dizziness or unsteadiness.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine increased phenytoin and carbamazepine exposure (AUC) in human studies, including patients with epilepsy; thought to reflect reduced metabolism and increased absorption.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Normal culinary use is unlikely to matter; concentrated extracts and 'bioavailability-enhancer' capsules are the concern.

interactions.effect: May increase theophylline levels and prolong its half-life.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine 20 mg/day for 7 days raised theophylline Cmax, AUC and half-life in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Normal culinary use is unlikely to matter; concentrated extracts and 'bioavailability-enhancer' capsules are the concern.

interactions.effect: May slow clearance of some CYP1A2-metabolised medicines (theophylline is the best-studied example).
interactions.mechanism: Inferred from the human theophylline study (theophylline is mainly cleared by CYP1A2); direct CYP1A2 data are limited.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase blood levels of propranolol.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine gave an earlier and higher propranolol peak and higher AUC in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor pulse and blood pressure if starting a piperine supplement.

interactions.effect: May raise blood levels of medicines cleared by CYP3A4 (e.g. cyclosporine, tacrolimus, some antiepileptics).
interactions.mechanism: Piperine inhibits human CYP3A4 in vitro; however it also activates PXR and can induce CYP3A4/MDR1 expression in human cells, so the net clinical effect may vary with dose and duration.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase absorption of P-glycoprotein substrate drugs such as digoxin or dabigatran.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine inhibits human P-gp in vitro and 20 mg/day for 10 days increased fexofenadine (a P-gp probe) Cmax and AUC in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Extra caution with narrow-margin P-gp substrates such as digoxin.

interactions.effect: May raise digoxin levels.
interactions.mechanism: Theoretical extrapolation: digoxin is a P-gp substrate and piperine inhibits P-gp in vitro and in a human fexofenadine study; no direct digoxin study found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase blood levels of nevirapine.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine 20 mg/day raised nevirapine Cmax and AUC substantially in a small crossover study in healthy men.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Do not change HIV medicine routines without your HIV clinician.

interactions.effect: May raise rifampicin blood levels.
interactions.mechanism: Piperine increased rifampicin blood levels in patients with tuberculosis; piperine is combined with rifampicin in at least one Indian product (Risorine).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Saffron
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda and cooking for general wellbeing of mood, skin and complexion.

safetyFlags.note: Low culinary doses appear tolerated, but higher doses are linked to uterine stimulation and miscarriage risk; avoid supplement doses in pregnancy.
Therapeutic doses (about 30 mg/day of extract) show little toxicity, but high doses (several grams) are toxic.
400 mg/day for a week lowered standing systolic and mean arterial pressure in healthy volunteers.

interactions.effect: May add slightly to antiplatelet medicines at supplement doses.
interactions.mechanism: Saffron extract inhibits human platelet aggregation in vitro; a human trial found no change in clotting tests at 200-400 mg/day, so clinical relevance is uncertain.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory add to bleeding risk with warfarin at high doses.
interactions.mechanism: Theoretical (in vitro antiplatelet activity); 200-400 mg/day did not change PT, PTT or coagulation factors in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May add to blood-pressure-lowering medicines at higher doses.
interactions.mechanism: 400 mg/day lowered standing systolic and mean arterial pressure in healthy volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Possible additive effects on mood-related brain chemistry.
interactions.mechanism: Proposed serotonergic mechanism of saffron's antidepressant effect; no interaction studies with SSRIs/SNRIs found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Do not use saffron supplements in place of prescribed treatment.

herbs.name: Sweet flag / Calamus
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the nervous system, speech and memory.

safetyFlags.note: Contains beta-asarone, which is genotoxic and a liver carcinogen in rodents. EMA HMPC recommends limiting beta-asarone exposure from herbal medicines (about 115 micrograms/day) and favouring low-asarone (diploid) varieties; the US FDA prohibits calamus and its oil/extract in food.
Because of the genotoxicity concerns above and lack of safety data, avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Traditionally given to children in some regions; asarone exposure limits are body-weight based, so children are relatively more exposed.

interactions.effect: May increase drowsiness with sleeping pills, benzodiazepines or barbiturates.
interactions.mechanism: Calamus oil and asarone potentiated barbiturate sleep in animals; ethanol extract shows CNS-depressant actions in rodents.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Avoid driving if drowsy.

herbs.name: Spikenard / Indian nard
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of sleep and the nervous system.

safetyFlags.note: Classified as hypno-sedative in Ayurveda; may cause drowsiness.

interactions.effect: May add to drowsiness from sleeping pills, benzodiazepines or other sedatives.
interactions.mechanism: Anxiolytic action in mice was blocked by flumazenil, indicating a GABA-benzodiazepine receptor mechanism; additive sedation is plausible.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Avoid driving if drowsy.

interactions.effect: May add to blood-pressure-lowering medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Lowered blood pressure in a small randomised study in people with high blood pressure.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Indian snakeroot
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the heart, circulation and calm sleep.
commonProducts: BP and sleep blends containing sarpagandha

safetyFlags.note: Contains reserpine, a prescription-strength drug that depletes noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin. Reserpine is contraindicated in people with a history of depression and in peptic ulcer or ulcerative colitis; it has long been linked to low mood (a 2023 systematic review found the evidence inconsistent), and can cause nasal congestion and slow heart rate. Use only under medical supervision.
Lowers blood pressure (reserpine is an established antihypertensive); can cause excessive drops when combined with other BP-lowering medicines.
Unexpected hypotension and bradycardia have occurred under anaesthesia in patients taking reserpine; the label advised stopping 1-2 weeks before elective surgery.
Reserpine passes into breast milk; LactMed prefers an alternative, especially with newborn or preterm infants.
People taking levodopa should avoid reserpine-containing products: reserpine reduces the response to levodopa (no dedicated drug_class key exists for antiparkinson medicines).

interactions.effect: Excitation and high blood pressure.
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine releases/depletes monoamines; the reserpine label states that adding reserpine in patients on MAO inhibitors can cause excitation and hypertension and the combination should be avoided.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination unless your doctor specifically approves it. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Severe drop in blood pressure and slow heart rate during anaesthesia.
interactions.mechanism: Reduced responsiveness to noradrenaline after catecholamine depletion by reserpine.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist about this herb; ask your doctor whether to pause the herbal product before planned surgery. The reserpine label advised stopping 1-2 weeks before elective surgery.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of irregular heart rhythm with digoxin.
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine label: concurrent use with digitalis may enhance arrhythmias.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of irregular heart rhythm (quinidine named on label).
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine label: use cautiously with quinidine because arrhythmias may be enhanced.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Blood pressure may fall too low; beta-blocker effects (slow pulse, tiredness) may be increased.
interactions.mechanism: Additive blood-pressure lowering; reserpine label notes additive CNS-depressant and cardiovascular effects with beta-blockers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood pressure and pulse.

interactions.effect: Blood pressure may fall too low.
interactions.mechanism: Additive antihypertensive effect (reserpine was marketed in fixed combination with thiazides).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Increased drowsiness and slowed reactions.
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine label: additive CNS-depressant effects with barbiturates and alcohol.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Avoid alcohol and driving if drowsy.

interactions.effect: May worsen low mood or reduce the benefit of antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine depletes brain monoamines and its label contraindicates use with a history of depression; however, a 2023 systematic review found its association with depression inconsistent. No specific interaction studies found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May worsen low mood or reduce the benefit of antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: Monoamine depletion by reserpine; label contraindication in depression; evidence on depression is inconsistent. No specific SSRI/SNRI interaction studies found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May reduce how well levodopa works.
interactions.mechanism: Reserpine in sarpagandha depletes dopamine; the levodopa label advises against reserpine.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Velvet bean
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the nervous and reproductive systems and vitality.
commonProducts: Mucuna extract capsules (often labelled with L-dopa %)

safetyFlags.note: Seeds naturally contain levodopa (L-dopa), the same active drug used in Parkinson's medicines; supplement levodopa content varies widely and is often not stated accurately. People taking levodopa/carbidopa, other dopaminergic medicines or dopamine-blocking medicines should not use it without their prescriber (no dedicated drug_class key exists for antiparkinson medicines).
An outbreak of acute toxic psychosis was attributed to eating Mucuna beans in Mozambique; levodopa can cause hallucinations and psychotic-like behaviour.
Contains levodopa; levodopa/carbidopa caused malformations in rabbits and there are no adequate human pregnancy data.
Levodopa can lower prolactin and may reduce milk supply.

interactions.effect: Dangerous rise in blood pressure (hypertensive reaction).
interactions.mechanism: Mucuna seed preparations deliver clinically active levodopa in humans; the FDA-approved levodopa label contraindicates non-selective MAO inhibitors. No study of Mucuna plus MAOIs exists, so severity rests on the regulatory contraindication for levodopa.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May reduce the effect of antipsychotics, and antipsychotics may block mucuna's dopamine effect; risk of worsening psychotic symptoms.
interactions.mechanism: Dopamine D2 antagonists reduce levodopa effect; levodopa can cause hallucinations/psychosis.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Dizziness or fainting from low blood pressure on standing.
interactions.mechanism: Symptomatic postural hypotension reported when levodopa was added to antihypertensive treatment (levodopa content of Mucuna).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Rise slowly from sitting or lying.

interactions.effect: Rare high blood pressure or abnormal movements.
interactions.mechanism: Rare reports of hypertension and dyskinesia with tricyclics plus levodopa.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Iron may reduce absorption of mucuna's levodopa.
interactions.mechanism: Iron salts reduce levodopa availability (levodopa label).
interactions.advice: Separate doses by at least 2 hours and talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Isoniazid may reduce the effect of mucuna's levodopa.
interactions.mechanism: Isoniazid can reduce the therapeutic effect of levodopa (levodopa label).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Phenytoin may reduce the effect of mucuna's levodopa.
interactions.mechanism: Phenytoin has been reported to reverse levodopa's effect (levodopa label).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Adds extra levodopa, which may cause unwanted movements, low blood pressure or confusion.
interactions.mechanism: Mucuna seeds naturally contain levodopa, in amounts that vary between products.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: False daisy
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the liver, hair and skin.

herbs.name: Ashoka tree
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the female reproductive system.
commonProducts: Women's wellness blends (e.g. with lodhra, shatavari)

safetyFlags.note: Commercial ashoka bark is frequently adulterated or substituted with other species (e.g. Polyalthia longifolia), so product content may not match the label.
Flower extract showed oestrogen-like activity in ovariectomised rats; no human pregnancy safety data.

interactions.effect: Could in theory add to or interfere with oestrogen-containing medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Oestrogenic activity of flower extract in ovariectomised rats; bark (the usual product) not tested in this way; no human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Lodh tree
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the female reproductive system and skin.

interactions.effect: Could in theory add to glucose-lowering medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Anti-diabetic activity reported in experimental studies of the stem bark (review); no human data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory interfere with hormonal medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Anti-androgenic activity reported in experimental studies (review); clinical relevance unknown.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Indian barberry (berberine)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the skin, eyes, liver and metabolism.
commonProducts: Blood-sugar and weight blends with berberine

safetyFlags.note: Berberine can displace bilirubin from albumin; authorities advise against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and in infants because of the risk to newborns.
Avoid exposing newborns to berberine via breast milk (bilirubin displacement concern).
Should not be given to infants/newborns, especially if jaundiced.
Lowers blood glucose; a case of severe hypoglycaemia with syncope was reported in a non-diabetic athlete using berberine supplements.

interactions.effect: Raises cyclosporine blood levels, risking toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: In kidney-transplant recipients, berberine 0.2 g three times daily raised cyclosporine trough levels and AUC (about 35% higher AUC); attributed to CYP3A4 and intestinal P-gp inhibition.
interactions.advice: Avoid unless your transplant team approves and monitors levels. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines (e.g. midazolam, tacrolimus, some statins).
interactions.mechanism: Berberine 300 mg three times daily for 2 weeks increased midazolam AUC about 40% in healthy men.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise levels of CYP2D6-metabolised medicines (e.g. some antidepressants, beta-blockers, dextromethorphan).
interactions.mechanism: Same human study: dextromethorphan/dextrorphan ratio rose about ninefold, indicating strong CYP2D6 inhibition.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise levels of CYP2C9-metabolised medicines (e.g. losartan, warfarin, some sulfonylureas).
interactions.mechanism: Same human study: losartan/E-3174 ratio doubled, indicating reduced CYP2C9 activity.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May change warfarin levels and bleeding risk.
interactions.mechanism: Extrapolated from CYP2C9 inhibition in humans; no direct warfarin study found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Check INR more often if you start or stop berberine.

interactions.effect: May increase absorption of P-gp substrate drugs.
interactions.mechanism: Berberine increased oral digoxin and cyclosporine bioavailability in rats via intestinal P-gp inhibition.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May raise digoxin levels.
interactions.mechanism: Dose-dependent increase in oral digoxin AUC/Cmax in rats (P-gp inhibition); no human study found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Digoxin levels may need checking.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: Additive glucose lowering (meta-analysis of trials); berberine also reported to act as an insulin secretagogue.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: Additive glucose lowering.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.effect: Additive glucose lowering; may slightly reduce metformin absorption at lower metformin doses.
interactions.mechanism: Goldenseal (berberine-containing) reduced metformin AUC by about 20% at low metformin doses but not overall in adults with type 2 diabetes; transporter (OCT/MATE) interactions shown in vitro.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

herbs.name: Indian kino tree
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of metabolism.

safetyFlags.note: Lowered fasting and post-meal glucose in an ICMR multicentre open trial; may cause low blood sugar with glucose-lowering medicines.

interactions.mechanism: Additive glucose lowering: clinical glucose reduction (ICMR trial) and combined effect with glibenclamide in diabetic mice.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

interactions.mechanism: Additive glucose lowering.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

herbs.name: Chirata
herbs.latin: Swertia chirata Buch.-Ham. ex Wall. (syn. S. chirayita)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda as a bitter for general wellbeing of digestion and the liver.

safetyFlags.note: Swerchirin, a chirata xanthone, strongly lowered blood glucose in rats, including tolbutamide-pretreated rats.
Widespread adulteration/substitution of commercial chirata has been reported.

interactions.effect: Could add to glucose lowering and cause low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: Swerchirin lowered blood glucose in rats including those pretreated with tolbutamide; no human interaction data.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

herbs.name: Indian frankincense / Boswellia
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of joints and mobility.

safetyFlags.note: Little is known about safety of medicinal oral doses in pregnancy or breastfeeding; food amounts are likely safe.
Not linked to liver enzyme elevations or clinically apparent liver injury in LiverTox.

interactions.effect: May increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
interactions.mechanism: Boswellia serrata is listed among herbs with published warfarin interaction case reports in a review; mechanism unclear (possibly CYP inhibition).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Check INR more often if you start or stop the herbal product.

interactions.effect: Could raise levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Frankincense extracts were potent, non-selective inhibitors of CYP1A2, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6 and 3A4 in vitro; boswellic acids inhibited CYP3A4 in rat microsomes.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could raise levels of CYP2C9-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: In vitro CYP2C9 inhibition by frankincense extracts.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could raise levels of CYP2D6-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: In vitro CYP2D6 inhibition by frankincense extracts.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could raise levels of CYP1A2-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: In vitro CYP1A2 inhibition by frankincense extracts.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could alter levels of P-gp substrate drugs.
interactions.mechanism: Boswellia extract and boswellic acids modulated P-gp transport in vitro; possible OATP1B3/MRP2 interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase glibenclamide (glyburide) levels and glucose lowering.
interactions.mechanism: Boswellic acids increased glyburide bioavailability and hypoglycaemic effect in diabetic rats.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Monitor blood glucose.

herbs.name: Malabar nut
herbs.latin: Justicia adhatoda L. (syn. Adhatoda vasica Nees)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the respiratory system.

safetyFlags.note: The alkaloid vasicine has oxytocic (uterine-stimulating) and abortifacient effects in animal studies; avoid in pregnancy.

herbs.name: Babchi
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the skin.

safetyFlags.note: Phototoxic: seeds contain psoralens; severe phototoxic burns have been reported (including in a child) when used with sun exposure. Avoid sun/UV exposure and do not combine with other photosensitising products without advice.
Acute hepatitis has been reported after oral babchi seeds; constituents such as bakuchiol and psoralen are hepatotoxic in animals.
Seed extracts and constituents show oestrogenic activity; no human pregnancy safety data.

interactions.effect: May add to liver strain from other liver-affecting medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Additive risk inferred from case reports of babchi hepatitis and hepatotoxic constituents in animals.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or abdominal pain promptly.

interactions.effect: May add to liver strain from isoniazid/rifampicin.
interactions.mechanism: Additive hepatotoxicity risk (theoretical), based on babchi hepatitis reports.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of sunburn-like skin reactions with photosensitising antibiotics (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones).
interactions.mechanism: Additive photosensitivity: psoralens are phototoxic, and these antibiotics are common photosensitisers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Avoid sun exposure.

interactions.effect: Could raise levels of CYP3A4-metabolised medicines.
interactions.mechanism: P. corylifolia extract and major components inhibited CYP3A4 in recombinant enzyme and human hepatoma cell models; constituents also inhibit UGT enzymes in vitro.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could in theory interfere with oestrogen-containing medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Oestrogenic activity of seed extracts and constituents in vitro.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Marking nut
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, only after purification (shodhana), for general wellbeing of joints and digestion.

safetyFlags.note: The fruit's tarry oil (urushiol-like bhilawanols, anacardic acid) causes blistering contact dermatitis; it is listed as a poisonous plant under India's Drugs and Cosmetics Act and must be purified before use.
Renal cortical necrosis with anuria was reported after exposure to marking-nut sap.
A probable DRESS-like severe drug reaction was reported after an oral formulation containing bhallataka.

interactions.effect: May add to kidney strain from other kidney-affecting medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Additive risk inferred from a case of renal cortical necrosis after sap exposure; no interaction studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Possible added kidney strain with regular NSAID use.
interactions.mechanism: Theoretical additive nephrotoxicity.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Nux vomica / Strychnine tree
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, only after purification and in very small doses, for general wellbeing of digestion and nerves.

safetyFlags.note: Contains strychnine and brucine, highly toxic alkaloids banned or severely restricted in most countries. Poisoning causes painful muscle spasms, seizure-like episodes, rhabdomyolysis and can be fatal; strychnine poisoning has been reported from traditional/therapeutic medicines.
Strychnine poisoning in a child from a therapeutic (traditional) medicine has been reported in India.
LiverTox notes nux vomica has not been shown to cause liver injury; the main danger is neuromuscular toxicity.

interactions.effect: May work against seizure control.
interactions.mechanism: Strychnine is a convulsant (glycine-receptor antagonist) that produces seizure-like muscle spasms; theoretical opposition to antiepileptic therapy.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbWarnings.effect: The herb itself has a very narrow safety margin; combining with any medicine makes problems harder to recognise.

herbs.name: Indian aconite
otherNames: Aconitum chasmanthum (species named in the API Vatsanabha monograph)
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, only after purification and in minute doses, within classical compound formulations.

safetyFlags.note: Aconite alkaloids (aconitine and related) are potent heart and nerve toxins. Poisoning causes numbness, vomiting, low blood pressure, slow or chaotic heart rhythm and can be fatal; cases have followed Ayurvedic aconite preparations, especially overdose or inadequate processing.
Severe hypotension, bradycardia and AV dissociation reported after Ayurvedic vatsanabha use.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of dangerous heart rhythm problems.
interactions.mechanism: Aconite causes ventricular arrhythmias; additive pro-arrhythmic risk with drugs that affect cardiac conduction is theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Higher risk of dangerous heart rhythm problems with digoxin.
interactions.mechanism: Both can cause arrhythmias and AV block; additive effect is theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Blood pressure and pulse may fall too low (especially with beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers).
interactions.mechanism: Aconite toxicity causes hypotension and bradycardia; additive effect is theoretical.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbWarnings.effect: The herb itself has a very narrow safety margin; combining with any medicine makes toxicity harder to recognise.

herbs.name: Thorn apple / Datura
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, only after purification and in minute doses, mainly within classical formulations.

safetyFlags.note: Contains tropane alkaloids (scopolamine/hyoscine, hyoscyamine) causing anticholinergic poisoning: dilated pupils, confusion, hallucinations, fast heart rate, high temperature and urinary retention. Poisonings occur from herbal teas and from Datura substituted into herbal medicines.
Children are at particular risk of anticholinergic poisoning from small amounts.
Scopolamine (a Datura alkaloid) may reduce milk production with long-term use.

interactions.effect: Stronger anticholinergic side effects: confusion, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate.
interactions.mechanism: Additive anticholinergic burden; tricyclics are strongly anticholinergic.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Stronger anticholinergic side effects and risk of confusion or overheating.
interactions.mechanism: Additive anticholinergic burden with anticholinergic antipsychotics.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: More constipation, urinary retention and drowsiness/confusion.
interactions.mechanism: Additive effects on gut motility, bladder and CNS (theoretical).
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: More confusion or drowsiness.
interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS effects (theoretical); benzodiazepines may be ineffective alone for Datura-induced delirium.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Unpredictable heart rate and confusion around anaesthesia.
interactions.mechanism: Antimuscarinic alkaloids (hyoscine/atropine-like) add to anticholinergic drugs used in anaesthesia (theoretical).
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist about this herb; ask your doctor whether to pause the herbal product before planned surgery.

herbWarnings.effect: The herb itself has a narrow safety margin and can cause delirium; combining with any medicine makes toxicity harder to recognise.

herbs.name: Asafoetida
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda, usually in small culinary amounts, for general wellbeing of the digestive system.
commonProducts: Hing (compounded powder, usually blended with flour)

safetyFlags.note: Case reports describe serious methaemoglobinaemia (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood) in infants given asafoetida as a home remedy; avoid giving it to infants.

interactions.effect: May slightly add to bleeding tendency alongside warfarin-type blood thinners.
interactions.mechanism: Asafoetida resin contains sesquiterpene coumarins; it is listed among herbs that could theoretically add to bleeding risk with warfarin. No clinical interaction reports found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding; your INR may need checking.

interactions.effect: May slightly add to bleeding tendency alongside newer oral blood thinners.
interactions.mechanism: Asafoetida resin contains sesquiterpene coumarins; it is listed among herbs that could theoretically add to bleeding risk with warfarin. No clinical interaction reports found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.effect: May slightly add to the anti-clotting effect of antiplatelet medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Asafoetida resin contains sesquiterpene coumarins; it is listed among herbs that could theoretically add to bleeding risk with warfarin. No clinical interaction reports found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.effect: May slightly add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect of these medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Hypotensive and smooth-muscle-relaxant activity reported in animal and laboratory studies only.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Watch for dizziness on standing.

herbs.name: Fennel
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the digestive system.

safetyFlags.note: The EU herbal monograph does not recommend medicinal fennel preparations during pregnancy because safety has not been established (estragole content). Normal culinary use is not covered by this caution.
Not recommended in medicinal amounts while breastfeeding per the EU monograph; trans-anethole passes into breast milk.

EU monograph: medicinal fennel not recommended under 4 years, and limited for ages 4-12 by estragole intake. Case reports link long-term fennel tea in infants to early breast development that resolved after stopping.
Avoid if allergic to plants of the carrot family (aniseed, caraway, celery, coriander, dill) or to mugwort pollen (cross-reactivity).

interactions.effect: Medicinal amounts of fennel taken at the same time may reduce absorption of ciprofloxacin-type antibiotics.
interactions.mechanism: In a rat study, fennel extract lowered ciprofloxacin peak levels by about 83% and exposure by about 48%, probably by metal-ion chelation. Animal data only; the EU monograph reports no human interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Your pharmacist may suggest taking the antibiotic a few hours apart from medicinal fennel preparations.

interactions.effect: Concentrated fennel products have weak oestrogen-like activity; the effect on hormonal medicines is unknown.
interactions.mechanism: Anethole and related compounds are considered weakly oestrogenic; supported by traditional reputation and paediatric case reports, not by interaction studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Green cardamom
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the digestive and respiratory systems.

interactions.mechanism: Aqueous cardamom extract inhibited human platelet aggregation in the test tube; a small uncontrolled study (3 g/day) reported increased fibrinolytic activity. No clinical interaction reports found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding; your INR may need checking.

herbs.name: Clove
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for general wellbeing of the digestive system and oral freshness.

safetyFlags.note: Clove oil (eugenol) in normal amounts has not been linked to liver injury, but swallowing large amounts, as in overdose, can cause severe liver injury.
Accidental swallowing of clove oil by young children has caused liver failure, seizures and clotting problems; keep clove oil out of reach of children.
Clove oil and its components (eugenol, acetyl eugenol) inhibit platelet aggregation in laboratory studies.

interactions.mechanism: Eugenol and acetyl eugenol inhibit platelet aggregation and thromboxane formation in vitro; clove is listed among herbs that could theoretically add to warfarin's effect. Concentrated clove oil/supplements are of more concern than culinary use.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding; your INR may need checking.

interactions.mechanism: Eugenol and acetyl eugenol inhibit platelet aggregation and thromboxane formation in vitro; clove is listed among herbs that could theoretically add to warfarin's effect. Concentrated clove oil/supplements are of more concern than culinary use.

interactions.effect: Large amounts of clove oil can injure the liver; combining with other liver-stressing medicines could theoretically add to this.
interactions.mechanism: Dose-related hepatotoxicity of eugenol in overdose; no interaction studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Avoid swallowing clove oil.

herbs.name: Nutmeg
herbs.traditionalContext: Traditionally used in Ayurveda in small amounts for general wellbeing of the digestive system and for restful sleep.

safetyFlags.note: Toxic in large doses: ingesting more than culinary amounts has caused hallucinations, agitation, fast heart rate, dry mouth, tremor and nausea, mainly attributed to myristicin.
Poison-centre data show unintentional nutmeg exposures in children under 13; store powders and products out of reach.

interactions.effect: Large amounts of nutmeg may add to drowsiness, confusion or other nervous-system effects of sedative medicines.

interactions.effect: Caffeine in green tea may reduce the effect of sedative medicines.

interactions.effect: Tea taken with iron tablets or folic acid can reduce how much is absorbed.

interactions.advice: Take iron or folic acid supplements a couple of hours apart from tea or green tea extract. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

herbs.name: Ginseng (Asian/Korean and American)
herbs.latin: Panax ginseng C.A.Mey.; Panax quinquefolius L. (root)
otherNames: not the same as ashwagandha ('Indian ginseng')
herbs.traditionalContext: Used in traditional East Asian medicine as a general tonic for energy and vitality.

safetyFlags.note: May be unsafe in pregnancy (a ginseng compound caused birth defects in animals); EU monograph does not recommend use in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Some experts advise against use in infants and children; EU monograph says use under 18 is not established.
May worsen autoimmune disorders.
May interfere with blood clotting.
May lower blood sugar.
Recognised perioperative concern because of effects on bleeding and blood sugar.

interactions.effect: May reduce warfarin's effect (lower INR), raising clot risk.
interactions.mechanism: Randomised trial: American ginseng reduced INR and warfarin levels in healthy volunteers; a case report describes a fall in INR with Panax ginseng.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Your INR may need checking more often if you start or stop ginseng.

interactions.effect: May add to the anti-clotting effect of antiplatelet medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Panaxynol from ginseng inhibited platelet aggregation in vitro (ginsenosides had little effect); NCCIH notes ginseng may interfere with clotting.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.effect: May add to the blood-sugar-lowering effect of this medicine, raising the chance of low blood sugar.
interactions.mechanism: American ginseng reduced post-meal blood glucose in people with and without type 2 diabetes in a small randomised study; NCCIH notes Asian ginseng may lower blood sugar.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. If you combine them, check your blood sugar more often and know the signs of low blood sugar.

interactions.effect: Reported to cause headache, tremor and manic-like symptoms with phenelzine.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May lower blood levels of medicines cleared by CYP3A4.
interactions.mechanism: Panax ginseng 500 mg twice daily for 28 days reduced midazolam exposure by about one-third (CYP3A induction) in healthy volunteers; P-gp was unaffected.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Your doctor may need to check drug levels.

interactions.effect: Reported liver injury when combined with imatinib.
interactions.mechanism: Case report of imatinib hepatotoxicity after 3 months of Panax ginseng energy drinks, possibly via CYP3A4 effects. LiverTox notes ginseng may cause herb-drug interactions leading to liver injury.
interactions.advice: Tell your oncology team before using ginseng. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Reported liver injury when combined with raltegravir-based HIV treatment.
interactions.mechanism: Case report of raised liver enzymes and jaundice (probable causality) in a patient on raltegravir plus lopinavir/ritonavir who took ginseng.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May contribute to liver injury when combined with other liver-affecting medicines.
interactions.mechanism: LiverTox: ginseng itself is not a recognised cause of liver injury but may cause interactions that lead to it.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Could theoretically work against immune-suppressing medicines.
interactions.mechanism: Immune-stimulating activity and possible worsening of autoimmune disorders (NCCIH); no interaction studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Ginseng can falsely raise or lower digoxin blood-test results with some laboratory methods.
interactions.mechanism: Digoxin-like immunoreactive components in ginseng interfere with certain digoxin immunoassays (assay interference, not a true level change).
interactions.advice: Tell the lab and your doctor you take ginseng if your digoxin level is being checked. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May increase bleeding and low-blood-sugar risk around surgery.
interactions.mechanism: Perioperative review: bleeding and hypoglycaemia are recognised direct effects of ginseng.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon or anaesthetist; they may advise pausing ginseng before a planned procedure.

herbs.name: St John's wort
herbs.traditionalContext: Used in European herbal tradition for general emotional wellbeing; included here as a reference herb because it interacts with many medicines.

safetyFlags.note: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; animal studies showed reproductive toxicity and breastfed infants may have side effects.
Can cause sensitivity to sunlight; avoid intense UV exposure while using it.
Not recommended under 18 years (insufficient data).
Interactions with anaesthesia medicines should be identified before elective surgery; it may need to be discontinued.

interactions.effect: Can sharply lower cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus or everolimus levels; organ-transplant rejection has occurred.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. The EU monograph contraindicates these combinations.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Do not start or stop St John's wort without your transplant team.

interactions.effect: Can reduce the effect of warfarin-type anticoagulants, raising clot risk.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. Contraindicated with coumarin-type anticoagulants in the EU monograph.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower rivaroxaban/apixaban levels and reduce protection against clots.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. The rivaroxaban label says to avoid combined P-gp and strong CYP3A inducers such as St John's wort.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can greatly lower levels of HIV medicines (e.g. protease inhibitors, nevirapine), risking treatment failure and resistance.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. Indinavir exposure fell markedly in volunteers; contraindicated with protease inhibitors and NRTIs in the EU monograph.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can reduce the effectiveness of birth-control pills and cause breakthrough bleeding; unplanned pregnancy is possible.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. Lowered ethinyl estradiol/progestin exposure and increased breakthrough bleeding in controlled studies.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method if combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of cancer medicines such as irinotecan, imatinib and docetaxel, making them less effective.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. Irinotecan active-metabolite levels fell by about 42% and imatinib exposure fell in clinical studies; contraindicated with cytostatics metabolised by these pathways.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Tell your oncology team about all supplements.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of narrow-margin CYP3A4 medicines, risking loss of effect.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May cause serotonin syndrome (agitation, sweating, fast heartbeat, fever, tremor) with SSRI/SNRI antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: Additive serotonergic effects; the EU monograph and NCCIH warn of serious serotonin-related side effects.
interactions.advice: Avoid this combination. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Seek urgent care for agitation, shaking, fever or a racing heart.

interactions.effect: May add to serotonin effects with MAO-inhibitor antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: Serotonergic activity; the EU monograph warns about combining with other serotonergic substances. No specific MAOI studies found.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of amitriptyline and related antidepressants.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. Amitriptyline is named among affected drugs.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower digoxin levels.
interactions.mechanism: P-glycoprotein induction; digoxin exposure fell by about 25% after 10 days of co-treatment in volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Your doctor may need to check digoxin levels.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of medicines carried by P-glycoprotein (e.g. digoxin, dabigatran, fexofenadine).
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower simvastatin (and other CYP3A4-cleared statin) levels.
interactions.mechanism: CYP3A4 induction; simvastatin acid exposure fell while pravastatin was unaffected in volunteers.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower methadone and oxycodone levels, reducing pain relief or triggering withdrawal.
interactions.mechanism: CYP3A4 induction; oxycodone exposure fell markedly in volunteers and methadone levels dropped in patients.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: Can lower theophylline levels, reducing its effect.
interactions.mechanism: Induction of CYP1A2; identified as a clinically significant interaction in a regulatory/systematic review of case reports.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Your doctor may need to check theophylline levels, especially if you stop St John's wort.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of medicines cleared by CYP2C19 (e.g. omeprazole, some antidepressants) and may increase activation of clopidogrel.
interactions.mechanism: St John's wort induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein, lowering blood levels of many medicines; the effect rises with hyperforin content and lasts about a week after stopping. The EU monograph lists CYP2C19 among the induced enzymes.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May add to sun sensitivity (burning, rash) caused by photosensitising medicines such as tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, thiazides, isotretinoin or amiodarone.
interactions.mechanism: Hypericin in St John's wort causes photosensitivity; the EU monograph advises avoiding intense UV exposure and NCCIH notes severe skin reactions after sun exposure. Additive effect with photosensitising drugs is inferred.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Use sun protection and avoid intense UV exposure.

interactions.effect: Can lower levels of medicines cleared by CYP2C9.

interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining. Report unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.effect: May increase liver toxicity of other medicines by changing how they are metabolised.
interactions.mechanism: LiverTox: not a convincing cause of liver injury itself, but may increase hepatotoxicity of other agents via interactions.
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.

interactions.effect: May alter the effect of anaesthesia and other medicines used around surgery.
interactions.mechanism: Enzyme induction affects many perioperative drugs; enzyme activity returns to normal about 1 week after stopping.
interactions.advice: Tell your surgeon or anaesthetist; they may advise pausing St John's wort before a planned procedure.

herbs.name: Rasa sindoor (mercuric sulphide)
otherNames: ingredients: purified mercury (parada) and sulphur (gandhaka), heated by kupipakva method -> red mercuric sulphide (HgS)
found in Brahmi vati, Mahayogaraj guggulu, Vatvidhwansan ras and many 'ras' products
herbs.traditionalContext: A processed mercury-sulphur preparation used in Ayurvedic rasa shastra as a component of herbo-mineral formulations.

safetyFlags.note: Is a mercury compound by design. Mercury and lead have been detected at levels far above safety limits in rasa shastra products; a mercury-sulphide Ayurvedic remedy (Rasa Karpura) caused severe mercury poisoning in an infant.

Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding unless a doctor advises otherwise: lead poisoning, including miscarriage, was reported in pregnant women using rasa shastra (metal-containing) Ayurvedic medicines.
Keep away from children; severe lead and mercury poisoning has been reported in children given Ayurvedic herbo-mineral remedies.
Mercury is toxic to the kidneys; avoid with kidney disease.

interactions.effect: may add to kidney damage risk with kidney-toxic medicines
interactions.mechanism: mercury content (mercuric sulphide); additive kidney toxicity is theoretical
interactions.advice: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining.
